newsitem.title: GERMANY: Sketches of Bundesbank council members.
newsitem.headline: Sketches of Bundesbank council members.

text.p: Worries that Germany might not meet membership criteria for the single European currency have grown recently after it emerged this week that the European Commission expected the country's debt to remain high.

A number of Bundesbank council members have spoken out in recent days, giving diverse views on whether Germany will meet criteria to join a European single currency at its scheduled 1999 start under the Maastricht Treaty.
Following are brief sketches of who the Bundesbank council members are and what they stand for.

HANS TIETMEYER, 65, president whose term expires in August 1999. Tietmeyer, a Christian Democrat (CDU), is a top ally of Chancellor Helmut Kohl. Known as monetary centrist, he joined bank board in January 1990 after career in Bonn ministries. Named president in October 1993. He wants strict interpretation of Maastricht Treaty and has pushed for stability pact. He said on March 14 it was not the right time to discuss delay in EMU, said it improbable for EMU to start without France, Germany.

JOHANN WILHELM GADDUM, 54, vice president whose term expires in June 1998. Gaddum, a CDU member and former president of the Rheinland-Palatinate bank, joined directorate in 1986 and appointed to job in October 1993. A centrist, he is expert on capital markets but has limited international exposure. Gaddum sympathetic to public fears about Euro and favours strict treaty interpretation. He favours stability pact with sanctions. But he has recently been silent in EMU debate.

OTMAR ISSING, 60, chief economist. Issing, a professor who has no political affiliation, joined council in October 1990 and is seen as a centrist on monetary issues. Issing is a proponent of the EMU stability pact and warns against softening EMU entry criteria. He also critical of "creative accounting" to fulfil fiscal critiera and cannot rule out Germany falling short of EMU criteria for 1996. Also recently silent on EMU.

WENDELIN HARTMANN, 59, directorate member for payment systems, controlling. Hartmann, a technical banking expert with no political affiliation, joined bank in 1964 and was appointed to directorate in June 1992. He chairs an EMI working group on coordinating cashless payments under EMU. Hartmann, an interest rate hawk, believes transition period between the Euro's introduction and physical distrubition should be shortened. Recently said talk of EMU delay was premature.

HELMUT SCHIEBER, 58, directorate member for international relations. Schieber, who has no political affiliation, joined bank in 1964 and directorate in June 1992. Schieber, a centrist on rate policy, believes EMU target start date for January 1999 will be hard to meet and entry criteria should not be relaxed. Has made no major public comment on EMU since February.

PETER SCHMIDHUBER, 65, directorate member for legal and administrative issues. Schmidhuber, a Christian Social (CSU) member, is ally of Finance Minister Waigel. Viewed as monetarist hawk, he joined directorate in March 1995. He believes timely start to EMU possible if steps made to ensure stability. Believes delay could endanger project but said in late February good financial track record needed to join.

EDGAR MEISTER, 56, directorate member in charge of banking supervision. Meister, a Social Democrat (SPD), joined directorate in 1993 and considered favourite to replace Gaddum. Meister, a monetarist dove, wants clear interpretation of entry criteria. He cites public confusion due to questions about how criteria will be interpreted and fears political pressure may push through the introduction of the new currency at any price. Quiet on EMU debate since late January.

KLAUS-DIETER KUEHBACHER, 53, President of Berlin and Brandenburg state central bank. Kuehbacher, a former Bundestag member, viewed as outspoken SPD politician and expert on fiscal policy, named in September 1995 to position. A monetarist dove, he wants EMU to start on time in 1999 with small group rather than risk delay or softening criteria. He said in March that he doubts Germany to reach goal of 1997 deficit under three percent but said deficit may not be most critical criteria.

FRANZ-CHRISTOPH ZEITLER, 48, President of Bavaria state central bank. Zeitler, a CSU supporter viewed as monetary centrist, appointed to post in 1995, oversaw in 1991 introduction of "solidarity surcharge" to pay for German unification. He is critical of nations using gimmicks to meet entry criteria but has so far steered clear of debate on postponing EMU launch.

REIMUT JOCHIMSEN, 63, President of North-Rhine Westphalia state central bank. Jochimsen, an SPD member and former professor, was economics minister of North-Rhine Westphalia before current position in August 1990. Jochimsen, monetarist centrist to dove, hit France for budget moves, says Germany will not accept the Euro if the criteria are relaxed. He said in February that budgetary fudging "order of the day" for EMU.

HANS-JUERGEN KOEBNICK, 58, President of Saarland and Rheinland-Palatinate state central bank. Koebnick, a former journalist and SPD mayor, named president of Saarland bank in 1991 and Rheinland-Pfalz bank in 1993. A monetarist dove, he sees forecasts that Germany may miss EMU criteria in 1997 as realistic. EMU delay may be useful and that Italy, Spain and other "Club Med" countries unlikely in first group. Few recent public comments in EMU debate.

GUNTRAM PALM, 65, President of Baden-Wuerttemberg state central bank. Palm, a CDU member, was state minister before named to current job in April 1992. A monetarist hawk, he warns against using tricks to join EMU. He favours criteria interpretation aimed at stability but among group who says deficit criteria may not be the most critical in creating long-term stable currency. He said in March that he believes EMU to start on time, any delay to cause sharp rise in mark.

ERNST WELTEKE, 54, President of Hesse state central bank. Welteke, an SPD member and former state economics and finance minister, was named to job in 1995. Welteke, a monetarist dove, believes EMU delay to enlarge group unwise and could threaten project. He sees some leeway in budget criteria but not laxity, believes EMU will start on time and that deficit criteria should not be a "knock-out" criteria for EMU membership.

OLAF SIEVERT, 63, President of Saxony and Thuringia state central bank. Sievert aligned with no political party, was professor before named to job in January 1993. Sievert, a monetarist dove, says EMU delay would be beginning of end, favours small group. Sees Euro helping solve European jobless. Few public comments on EMU debate but said in January that he favours independent and neutral European Central Bank.

HANS-JUERGEN KRUPP, 63, President of Schleswig-Holstein and Hamburg and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern state central bank. Krupp, an SPD member and monetarist dove, was president of DIW institute. Named to current post in December 1993. Krupp says nations do not need to hit debt criteria exactly to qualify and sees room to manoeuvre, particularly on public debt. Few recent public comments about EMU.

HELMUT HESSE, 62, President of Lower Saxony and Bremen and Saxony Anhalt bank. Hesse, who has no political affiliation, is Club of Rome member. Was named bank president in December 1988 and given responsibility for more regional banks in November 1992. Hesse said on March 13 that Germany should not be able to join currency union if it fails to meet entry criteria.
